profile.reading:
WA12 is one of the data center buildings on Vantage Data Centers' Quincy campus in Grant County, Washington, near the town of Quincy in the Columbia River basin of central Washington. Vantage's own site lists the campus address as 2101 M Street NE, Quincy, WA 98848, describes the site as a 68 acre campus with about 775,000 square feet of data center space split across three buildings, and states the campus carries 89 MW of critical IT load in total. WA12 is named specifically on Vantage's site alongside WA11 in the list of Uptime Institute Tier III certifications, Tier III certification of design documents, Tier III certification of the constructed facility, and Tier III Gold certification of operational sustainability, along with LEED Gold certification from the U.S. Green Building Council, and WA12 also appears in image captions and feature copy on power, cooling, connectivity, and security for the campus. No building specific square footage or IT load figure broken out for WA12 alone was found, since Vantage publishes those numbers only as a campus total across all three buildings, so no individual numeric figure is recorded for this building beyond the certifications named above.

The reason a data center campus exists in a farming town of a few thousand people in central Washington is electricity. Grant County is served by Grant County Public Utility District, a publicly owned power utility that holds physical rights to 63.31 percent of the combined output of the Priest Rapids and Wanapum hydroelectric dams on the Columbia River, two projects with more than 2,100 MW of combined generating capacity, part of why the region markets itself as having some of the lowest industrial electricity rates in the country. Grant PUD's own public materials describe serving eight data center operators across the county, drawing roughly 280 average megawatts between them, about 37 percent of the utility's total 757 MW system load as of 2025, and state that large power users, including data centers, are billed for the cost of the additional generation and infrastructure their load requires rather than sharing residential rates. The utility also discloses roughly 800 MW of pending large load applications still working through planning, procurement, permitting, and construction, a sign of continued demand pressure from data center developers drawn to the area's hydropower. Grant PUD's materials describe the county's data center customers in aggregate rather than naming individual operators or facilities, so no utility sourced figure specific to Vantage or to this building was found, and none is recorded here as a building level number.

Vantage Data Centers is a wholesale and hyperscale data center developer and operator with campuses across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific, and Quincy is one of several Vantage sites in the Columbia Basin hydropower corridor of central Washington, a corridor that also draws other large computing operators for the same utility economics. A third building on the same campus, referred to elsewhere as WA13, sits immediately adjacent to WA12 and is reasonably read as the remaining building the campus page counts toward its three building, 775,000 square foot total, though Vantage's site does not itemize certifications for it by name the way it does for WA11 and WA12. No Grant County parcel record or construction permit specific to WA12 was identified in this pass, so its individual construction timeline and completion date are not recorded here.

reading.body:
WA12 is one of three buildings on Vantage Data Centers' Quincy campus in central Washington, a 68-acre site near the Columbia River that Vantage describes as holding 89 MW of critical IT load across 775,000 square feet total. Vantage publishes no per-building breakdown, so WA12's individual capacity is unknown, though the campus figure of 89 MW suggests roughly 1,400 to 2,200 racks across all three buildings, depending on whether the IT load runs at 40 to 60 kW per rack, a range spanning both AI training density and hyperscale general compute. WA12 holds Uptime Institute Tier III certifications for design, construction, and operations, Tier III Gold for operational sustainability, and LEED Gold from the U.S. Green Building Council, qualifications appropriate for critical infrastructure serving large-scale compute tenants.

Grant County Public Utility District, which serves the Quincy site, draws on the Priest Rapids and Wanapum hydroelectric dams' combined 2,100-plus MW of generation capacity and reports serving eight data center operators across the county at roughly 280 average megawatts combined, representing 37 percent of the county's total 757 MW system load as of 2025. The utility does not name individual operators or sites in its public disclosures, so Vantage's share of county load is not published. Grant PUD also reports roughly 800 MW of pending large-load applications still in planning and permitting, a figure that signals continued developer interest in the region's hydropower-backed low-cost electricity despite the power already committed to existing data center operators.

This Quincy campus ranks third by published megawatts across Washington state, behind only two other named facilities, though Washington has 46 mapped data centers, of which only 2 publish capacity figures. WA12's position on a large, purpose-built campus with certified redundancy and proven power access makes it relevant to any operator evaluating where grid constraints will bind AI scaling, but the lack of building-level published specifications prevents detailed assessment of its role in that scaling relative to the other two buildings on the same campus.
